name: Hip flexor stretch
equipment: folded towel or cushion for back knee
noEquipmentAlternative: Standing hip flexor stretch in a long split stance holding a desk or wall

metOptions.activity: MET: 2.3, from the 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities, code 02101, "stretching, mild". The same value was used in the 2011 edition. The search could not confirm whether the 2024 value is mea

prescriptions.reps: 30 s hold per side (standing, desk break)
5 breaths per side (Anjaneyasana, hands on blocks)
45-60 s hold per side or couch stretch

formChecks.message: Leaning forward: stack your shoulders over your hips
Squeeze your back glute and shift your hips forward
Move your front foot further forward

formChecks.rule: pelvis rotated (front view hip width shrinks > 30%)
formChecks.message: Square your hips to the front

progressions: Half-kneeling with same-side arm overhead and side bend
Anjaneyasana with arms up and gentle backbend
Couch stretch (back shin against wall or sofa)
regressions: Standing hip flexor stretch holding desk or wall
Half-kneeling with both hands on a chair and thick knee cushion

videoShots.shows: padding the knee and setting up half-kneeling with front knee at 90 deg
videoShots.textOverlay: Pad the back knee. Front knee over ankle.

videoShots.shows: pelvic tuck with low back flattening
glute squeeze and whole-body forward shift, torso upright
square hips and front knee over middle toes

setupSteps: Put the mat lengthwise in a clear area, near a wall, sofa arm or sturdy chair you can touch for balance.
Fold a towel in two or three layers, or use a cushion, and place it where your back knee will go. Kneeling on bare tile is uncomfortable and can irritate the kneecap.
Kneel on both knees on the padding, upright, with your knees hip-width apart (about 15 to 20 cm, est.).
Step your RIGHT foot forward so it is flat on the floor and your right knee is bent to about 90°, with the knee roughly over the ankle (University of Michigan Health/Healthwise; Yoga Journal).
Keep your LEFT knee on the padding directly under or slightly behind your left hip, with the top of your left foot or the toes on the mat, pointing straight back. Do not turn the foot out.
Set the width. Your feet should sit as if on "train tracks" about hip-width apart, not on a tightrope, so you can balance.
Stack your torso upright: shoulders over hips, eyes forward, hands on hips or one hand on the chair or wall.
Point the front of your pelvis forward. Both hip bones should face the front wall, level, with no twist.
Stand facing your desk or a wall and hold it lightly.
Step your LEFT foot back into a long walking stride, about 60 to 90 cm (est.). Point both feet forward.
Raise the back heel so you are on the ball of the back foot. Keep the back knee straight or only slightly bent.
Optional (NHS Wrightington, Wigan and Leigh handout): put the front foot on a stair or step and use the banister for support.
From Downward Dog or all-fours, step the right foot forward between your hands with the knee over the heel.
Lower the left knee onto padding and slide it back until you feel a gentle stretch at the front of the left thigh and groin (Yoga Journal).
Rest the fingertips on blocks, books or the floor beside the front foot to start.

steps.title: Brace the trunk
steps.action: tighten your stomach gently, as if about to be poked, without holding your breath.
steps.feel: a light firmness around the waist.
steps.visualCheck: side view, the rib cage sits over the pelvis and is not flared. Front view, the shoulders are level.

steps.title: Tuck the pelvis (backward tilt)
steps.action: point your tailbone down toward the floor and lift the front of the pelvis toward your belly button, as if tucking a tail between your legs. Yoga Journal uses the same cue for Anjaneyasana.
steps.feel: an early stretch at the very front of the LEFT hip, and maybe right away.
steps.visualCheck: side view, the low-back curve flattens slightly and does not increase.

steps.title: Squeeze the back-leg buttock
steps.visualCheck: side view, the left thigh moves slightly behind the line of the torso.

steps.title: Shift forward
steps.action: move your whole body slowly forward a few centimetres, bending more at the front knee, until you feel a mild-to-moderate stretch, about 4 to 6 out of 10 (est.). Do not lean the torso forward.
steps.feel: a stretch at the front of the left hip and upper thigh, not in the low back and not sharp in the knee.
steps.visualCheck: side view, the torso stays upright or vertical and the hips travel forward. Front view, the pelvis stays square and the front knee tracks over the second and third toes.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay still, keeping the tuck, brace and squeeze.
steps.feel: the stretch may ease a little over the hold. If it fades, shift a few millimetres further.
steps.breathing: slow nasal breathing, about 4 seconds in and 4 to 6 seconds out (est.).
steps.visualCheck: no arching, no twisting, shoulders relaxed down.

steps.title: Optional: add the arm reach (deeper, and the start of the yoga version)
steps.action: raise your LEFT arm (same side as the back knee) overhead and lean very slightly to the right.
steps.feel: the stretch spreads up the left side of the trunk.
steps.breathing: breathe in as the arm rises.
steps.visualCheck: the ribs do not pop forward and the low back does not arch.

steps.title: Come out
steps.action: lower the arm, release the buttock squeeze, and slide the hips back over the back knee.

steps.title: Switch sides
steps.action: put a hand on the front knee or the chair, bring the front foot back to kneeling, then step the left foot forward.
steps.visualCheck: the padding is under the new back knee.

commonMistakes.title: Arching the low back instead of stretching the hip
commonMistakes.text: Arching the low back instead of stretching the hip. The hip flexors pull the pelvis forward, so the low back "gives" and the stretch is lost, and it may strain the back. Fix: tuck the tailbone and brace the stomach before shifting forward. Several sources, including ACE, Physitrack and prehab libraries, flag this.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning the torso forward
commonMistakes.text: Leaning the torso forward. Bending forward over the front leg shortens the hip flexors again. Fix: keep the shoulders stacked over the hips, think "tall", and move the whole body forward as one unit.

commonMistakes.title: Twisting the pelvis open
commonMistakes.text: Twisting the pelvis open. The back-leg hip swings backward and the stretch moves away from the target. Fix: keep both hip bones facing forward (ACE: pelvis level, no rotation). Placing a hand on each hip bone helps you feel it.

commonMistakes.title: Back foot turned outward (standing version)
commonMistakes.text: Back foot turned outward (standing version). This changes which muscles stretch and lets the hip rotate. Fix: point both feet straight forward (prehab library cue).

commonMistakes.title: Pushing into pain
commonMistakes.text: Pushing into pain. Going too far triggers protective tightening and can irritate the front of the hip or the knee. Fix: aim for a mild-to-moderate pull, never a sharp pain. Every NHS trust handout reviewed says to stop if the stretch causes pain.

commonMistakes.title: Bare knee on a hard floor
commonMistakes.text: Bare knee on a hard floor. Pressure on the kneecap is painful and makes people rush. Fix: use a folded towel or cushion (South Tees and Columbia/NYP handouts).

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. This raises tension and can raise blood pressure. Fix: breathe slowly through the nose throughout the hold.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing. Bouncing in a static stretch is not recommended for beginners. Fix: move slowly into position and hold still.

safetyNotes: Knee problems (pain kneeling, kneecap or meniscus issues, arthritis): pad the back knee well or use the standing version instead. Avoid deep front-knee bending if it hurts.

Hip problems: this includes recent hip replacement, hip impingement (FAI), labral tears, and groin or hip flexor strain. Get clearance from your surgeon or physio first, because hip extension and rotation limits often apply after hip replacement. Stop if you feel a pinching pain at the front of the hip.
Low back pain: keep the pelvis tucked and the stretch small. If the stretch increases back pain, stop and seek advice.
High blood pressure or heart conditions: avoid long holds with the arms overhead in Anjaneyasana. Keep your hands on your hips and keep breathing, never hold the breath.

Pregnancy: the gentle standing version with support is usually tolerated, but balance changes and ligaments loosen. One yoga source advises avoiding Anjaneyasana in pregnancy and after giving birth. Ask your antenatal care provider, avoid overstretching, and always use support.
Recent surgery (abdominal, hernia, hip, knee): wait for medical clearance.
Balance problems or dizziness: do it next to a wall or chair, or use the edge-of-bed version.

Stop immediately if you feel: sharp or stabbing pain; pins and needles, numbness or burning down the leg; pain in the kneecap; low-back pain that builds; dizziness; or a "pop" or clicking with pain at the front of the hip.
Gym etiquette: use the stretching area rather than the walkway, wipe the mat afterwards, and do not hog the space during busy hours.

Hold time: sources range from 5 s × 10 (NHS WWL) through 15 to 30 s (Healthwise, ACSM) to 30 to 45 s (ACE). We chose 30 s × 2 to 3 per side to meet ACSM's ~60 s total.

Front knee past the toes: some yoga sites say never let it pass the toes. Yoga Journal and Healthwise put the knee over the ankle or heel. We chose "knee roughly over the ankle; slight forward travel during the shift is fine if it is pain-free" (est.).

Pelvis cue: Physitrack says keep the pelvis "neutral". Yoga Journal, the NHS WWL handout and prehab libraries say tuck the tailbone. We chose a gentle tuck, because the 2024 trial suggests the posterior tilt changes the stretch's effect and it protects against arching.
Which muscle is stretched: the standard lunge mainly targets the iliopsoas. Bending the back knee (couch stretch) adds the rectus femoris, so we listed the couch stretch as a progression.
Pregnancy: one yoga source says avoid Anjaneyasana. Others are silent. We advise the supported standing version and checking with the antenatal provider.
